title: Monolith, microservices or serverless?

rows.label: In one line
values: One application, deployed as one unit
Many small services, each deployed on its own and owning its data
Managed services plus functions the platform runs only when an event arrives

rows.label: Unit of deployment
values: The whole app; every change ships everything
One service; teams ship on their own schedules
One function (or a small group); the platform handles servers

rows.label: How it scales
values: Run more identical copies behind a load balancer; the shared database is the limit
Scale each service separately, only where load is
The platform starts instances per event and scales to zero when idle (Lambda: 1,000 concurrent executions per Region by default, raisable)

rows.label: Calls between parts
values: Function calls in one process: nanoseconds, no failure modes of their own
Network calls (HTTP, gRPC) or messages: milliseconds, and they can fail or time out
Events, queues and workflow services; every hop is a network call, and some are billed per call

rows.label: Data
values: One database; one transaction can cover several features
A database per service; cross-service changes need sagas and eventual consistency
Kept in managed services; a function shouldn’t rely on state between invocations

rows.label: Built-in limits
values: Build and test time grow with the codebase
Latency adds up along chains of synchronous calls
Lambda runs at most 15 minutes per invocation; cold starts hit under 1% of invocations and take from under 100 ms to over a second

rows.label: Cost shape
values: A few always-on instances; cheap to run and to understand
Instances per service plus the platform (pipelines, monitoring, tracing) every service needs
Per request and per millisecond; idle costs nothing, but steady high load can cost more than always-on containers

rows.label: Debugging
values: One process, one log stream, one profiler
Distributed tracing to follow a request across services
Distributed tracing, plus local emulators or deploys to test the wiring

rows.label: Fits
values: New products, and one to a few teams; modular monoliths stretch much further
Many teams with stable domain boundaries and mature automation
Event-driven glue, spiky or low traffic, scheduled jobs and small APIs

rows.label: Known examples
values: Basecamp; Shopify’s modular Rails monolith (2.8 million lines in 2020)
Amazon.com (100+ services per page in 2006); Netflix (hundreds of microservices by 2016)
Prime Video’s stream monitor started serverless, then moved to one process and cut cost by over 90%

tip: These are not stages you must pass through. Most systems should start as a well-structured monolith and split off a service only when a team or a part of the load clearly needs its own lifecycle; Fowler’s rule of thumb is not to consider microservices unless the system is too complex to manage as a monolith. Serverless functions fit around either style, for jobs triggered by events. Mixes are normal: a monolith with a few functions for image resizing and webhooks is a common, healthy shape.
